strengths: This work focuses on defending against black-box MI attacks which have not been addressed in the existing defense.
As a post-processing defense, SSD can be easily integrated with most pre-trained models for defending against black-box attacks.
Empirical results demonstrate SSD's success in reducing the attack performance of four state-of-the-art black-box MI attacks.
This paper considers defense against model inversion attack from a new perspective by proposing CMI, which provides new insights into this field.
It provides thorough theoretical analysis to support the effectiveness of the SSD defense, with a clear and rigorous logical structure.
The paper achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of utility-privacy trade-off and defense against advanced black-box attacks, qualitatively demonstrating its effectiveness.
The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
The idea behind the proposed defense is intuitive and presented well.
Experiments seem comprehensive and the defense shows better utility-privacy tradeoff compared to prior defenses in both soft and hard label settings
The defense is post-processing based, making it easy to adopt.
The authors propose SSD, a post-processing defense mechanism that doesn’t require retraining the model, making it practical for real  deployment.

The authors theoretically prove that minimizing CMI serves as a special information bottleneck, therefore minimizing CMI can effectively balance data privacy and utility. By iterating the CMI through all possible labels, the whole dataset can thus be.
The paper introduces an adaptive rate-distortion mechanism optimized using the water-filling method. This approach efficiently calibrates the probability distributions output by the model.

The authors validate their method across various attack algorithms (BREP, Mirror, C2F, LOKT), datasets (FaceScrub, CelebA), and model architectures (VGG-16, IR-152). The results demonstrate that SSD outperforms existing defenses in terms of defense scheme robustness and effectiveness on preservation of model utility.
weaknesses: Practical limitations: the proposed method requires a validation dataset D_{valid} that must be real data, raising concerns about data leakage and robustness of the estimated conditional mutual information, especially when per-class validation sets have few samples or only a single sample per class.

SSD's prediction process involves an optimization step for each image, leading to significantly increased computational costs and slower inference times, making the method impractical for real-time applications or large-scale deployments and raising concerns about energy consumption.
The experiments were conducted on low-resolution 64x64 images, limiting the generalizability of the findings to high-resolution scenarios that are more common in real-world applications.

The paper suffers from some typos and grammatical errors. For examples, lines 41, 107.

Key concepts, such as the water-filling method, lack adequate coverage in the main body; its omission hinders a comprehensive understanding of the core methodology and its impact on the optimization process.
The experimental setup omits certain critical information, such as the dataset used for GAN prior training and the exact hyperparameters for Figure 1, raising concerns about reproducibility.

The study exclusively benchmarks against state-of-the-art white-box defenses but omits comparisons with black-box defenses, weakening the claim of achieving state-of-the-art performance in the black-box setting.
There are also minor errors, such as duplicated words (line 107), inconsistent notation (duplicate use of $p$ at line 215) and typo at line 314.
The notation is unconventional, such as using non-bold font for vector inputs like \mathbf{x}, which reduces consistency with standard notation practices.

The proposed defense could be susceptible to an adaptive attack where an adversary queries the same input multiple times and averages the noisy outputs to cancel the added noise; this vulnerability is not discussed in the paper.

The defense requires a validation dataset to implement, which could limit its adoption in scenarios where such a dataset is not readily available, making the defense less flexible and harder to deploy in real-world settings.

Even though the authors claim that the computational overhead is negligible due to the efficient optimization on GPU, a more detailed analysis or benchmarking of the computational cost would greatly support this claim.

Using MI/CMI in deep learning is gaining increasing attention, but its introduction in related work lacks both depth and breadth, making it hard to locate the role of this work within the relevant community.

The authors should use a deeper model architecture and higher-dimensional input data for training and prove the effectiveness of the proposed method; optimizing I(X;Ŷ ∣ Y) may be challenging when the input is high-dimensional and the model depth is large.
The authors should discuss the potential possibility of adaptive attacks and, if they deem such attacks unlikely, provide a justification for that assessment.
